companyCaseStudy.title: How Twitch Kept Millions Talking — Scaling Chat to Handle Millions of Concurrent Viewers
companyCaseStudy.summary: At peak times Twitch supports millions of concurrent viewers and chatrooms that can flood with tens of thousands of messages per second. Twitch rebuilt its chat stack to partition state, push most work to ephemeral stateless routing tiers, and adopt durable messaging to keep latency low and reliability high — cutting p99 delivery latency, reducing server hot‑spots, and surviving traffic spikes from viral streams.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook
When a top streamer goes live, Twitch chat explodes — rooms with 100k+ concurrent chatters and bursts of tens of thousands of messages per second. A single viral stream can push infrastructure from quiet to tens of millions of events in minutes. Twitch needed chat to stay snappy (sub‑second message delivery), reliable (no message loss), and cheap enough to scale with unpredictable spikes.

## Problem
- Chat is a many‑to‑many, real‑time fanout problem: one message must be delivered to tens to hundreds of thousands of subscribers. Naively fanouting from a single process quickly creates network and CPU hot spots.
- Presence (who’s in a room), moderation, and per‑room rate limits are stateful and hard to shard safely.
- Traffic is highly bursty: an esports final or a popular raid produces multi‑order magnitude spikes.

## Challenge
Twitch needed to answer three engineering questions:
1. How to partition rooms so no single server becomes a hot spot?
2. How to keep delivery latency under 1s (p50/p95/p99) under huge bursts?
3. How to keep chat fault‑tolerant — lose a node but don’t lose messages or clients?

## Solution — architectural approach
Twitch moved from a single stateful chat cluster toward a tiered, partitioned, and message‑brokered system with these core ideas:
- Partition rooms (channels) to chat shards so each shard owns presence & moderator state for a subset of rooms.
- Keep many stateless routing and websocket proxy tiers in front (autoscaled) to accept client connections and forward published messages to the right shard.
- Use a durable, distributed pub/sub/messaging backbone (Kafka/streaming system) for durable ingestion and asynchronous fanout when needed.
- Push per‑client delivery to horizontally scalable websocket proxy pools that subscribe to shard streams, reducing coupling between message ingestion and client connections.
- Implement backpressure and message coalescing for very high throughput rooms (batching messages where appropriate) and per‑room rate limiting for moderation.

High level architecture (simplified):

```mermaid
graph LR
  Client[User Websocket] -->|WS| WsProxy[Websocket Proxy (auto-scaled)]
  WsProxy -->|Publish msg| Ingest[Ingest Gateways]
  Ingest -->|To pub/sub| StreamBroker((Kafka / PubSub))
  StreamBroker --> ChatShard1[Chat Shard A (presence, moderation)]
  StreamBroker --> ChatShard2[Chat Shard B]
  ChatShard1 -->|Fanout| FanoutWorkers[Fanout Pool]
  FanoutWorkers --> WsProxy
  ChatShard2 --> FanoutWorkers
  ChatShard1 -->|Durable archive| LongTermStore[(S3 / HDFS)]
  WsProxy -->|Presence heartbeat| PresenceStore[(Redis clusters)]
```

### Key design decisions and why they matter
- Partition by channel id (consistent hashing + overflow rules): avoids single‑room hot spots by allowing shards to be rebalanced. When a channel becomes viral it can be rebalanced to more capacity or moved to a special high‑capacity cluster.
- Separate "ingest" from "delivery": clients push to ingest gateways which write to the broker (durable, replicated). Shards and fanout workers subscribe to broker topics. This decouples spikes in writes from client delivery and enables replays for late joiners.
- Use ephemeral websocket proxies that only manage TCP connections and subscriptions (no heavy per‑room business logic) so proxies can be scaled independently and replaced without losing global room state.
- Use Redis (or other in‑memory store) for fast presence checks and short‑lived per‑room counters. Durable storage (S3/Kafka) for archiving chat and moderation audit logs.

## Before vs After (representative numbers)
| Metric | Before | After |
|--------|--------:|------:|
| Max room fanout per server | ~50k users (hot‑spot risk) | Sharded; no single server > 10k active rooms |
| Burst handling | Overloaded, reply floods & dropped messages | Sustained spikes with <1% drop; degraded to batching only in extreme spikes |
| p99 message delivery latency | 2–5s during spikes | ~700ms (typical), <1.5s under extreme bursts |
| Mean operational incidents from chat floods | Multiple/week during big events | Incidents reduced by ~70% during major events |

## Operational details and tricks
- Autoscaling: websocket proxy pools scale by connection count and CPU; ingest and fanout pools scale by input rate and consumer lag in the broker.
- Hot channel mitigation: when a single channel exceeds thresholds it can be routed to a specialized fast‑path cluster with more memory, tuned batching, and dedicated fanout workers.
- Backpressure & client hints: proxies return rate limit hints and preferred batching windows to clients. Clients implement local coalescing for emotes and repeated messages.
- Moderation pipeline: moderation decisions are enforced in the shard owning the room; moderation events are also written to the broker and archived for auditing.

## Results (real world impact)
- Twitch went from frequent chat outages during high‑profile events to handling millions of concurrent viewers with chat latency kept under 1s for p95 in normal operation.
- Viral streams that used to cause large numbers of dropped messages are now mitigated with hot‑channel routing and burst batching, eliminating many operational fire drills.
- The separation of concerns (ingest vs delivery vs presence) made capacity planning simpler — scaling one tier no longer forced changes across the stack.

## Example operational flow (story)
When a streamer goes viral:
1. Client connections are absorbed by the websocket proxy pool — proxies scale horizontally.
2. Messages published by clients hit the ingest gateways, which append them to the durable broker.
3. Broker topic lag triggers additional fanout workers and may trigger rebalancing rules for the channel's shard.
4. Fanout workers push batches to subscribed websocket proxies which then write to clients. If proxies fall behind, broker retains messages for replay and proxies catch up.

## Table: Options considered vs chosen approach
| Option | Pros | Cons | Chosen? |
|--------|------|------|--------:|
| Single stateful cluster owning all rooms | Simple consistency | Hot spots, single point of failure | No |
| Stateless proxies + durable broker + sharded state | Decouples concerns; durable | More moving parts, operational complexity | Yes |
| Peer‑to‑peer fanout (clients relay) | Saves server bandwidth | Hard moderation, client trust issues | No |

## Why this is portable to other real-time problems
The same pattern (partition state, durable ingestion, stateless connection proxies, autoscaled fanout workers) maps to notifications, multiplayer game state, and live auctions — anywhere you need many‑to‑many low‑latency delivery under bursty load.
keyTakeaways: Separate concerns: ingest (durable writes), state (shards owning presence/moderation), and delivery (stateless websocket proxies + fanout) to avoid hot spots and reduce blast radius.
Use a durable broker (Kafka or equivalent) between ingest and fanout so you can autoscale consumers, replay missed messages, and absorb write bursts.
Detect hot channels and route them to special fast‑path clusters or enable batching/backpressure — this keeps p99 latency predictable during viral spikes.

concept.title: How Consistent Hashing Keeps Shards Stable When Nodes Come and Go
concept.summary: When you shard data (caches, partitions, or services), adding or removing nodes can trigger massive data reshuffling. Consistent hashing minimizes that churn so you can scale and fail gracefully without a complete rebalance.
concept.explanation:
## WHY it matters

Imagine you run a distributed cache or a partitioned database and you need to add a server (or one dies). With naive hashing, almost every key may need to move — causing cache storms, lots of network traffic, and degraded performance. *Consistent hashing* solves this by ensuring only a small fraction of keys move when the cluster changes.

**Analogy:** Think of a circular bulletin board (a town noticeboard arranged in a ring). Each house (node) hangs a mailbox at different points around the board. Each message (key) is pinned to the first mailbox clockwise from its hash. If a house moves in or out, only the messages between its neighbors need to be re-pinned — most notices stay put.

---

## How it works (intuitively)

- Hash nodes to points on a ring (0..2^32-1 or similar).
- Hash keys to points on the same ring.
- A key belongs to the first node clockwise from the key's point.
- When a node is added/removed, only keys mapped to the region between that node and its predecessor move.

### Mermaid: Ring lookup flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Client[Client Request (key)] --> HashKey([Hash(key)])
  HashKey --> FindPoint([Locate point on ring])
  FindPoint --> NodeA[Node A]
  FindPoint --> NodeB[Node B]
  FindPoint --> NodeC[Node C]
  subgraph Ring[Consistent Hash Ring]
    NodeA
    NodeB
    NodeC
  end
  NodeA -->|Serve| Client
  NodeB -->|Serve| Client
  NodeC -->|Serve| Client
```

### Sequence diagram: lookup & node change

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Router: GET key
  Router->>Ring: hash(key) -> find successor node
  Ring-->>Router: NodeX
  Router->>NodeX: request key
  NodeX-->>Router: value
  Router-->>Client: value

  Note over Router, Ring: NodeY added
  Ring->>Router: minimal remapping (~1/N of keys)
```

---

## Before / After: naive modulo vs consistent hashing

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| Modulo (key % N) — BEFORE | Extremely simple | Adding/removing N changes mapping for almost all keys (huge churn) | Stable small clusters, static node sets |
| Consistent Hashing — AFTER | Only ~K/N of keys move on node change; scalable, graceful | Slightly more complex; needs virtual nodes for balance; needs good hashing | Dynamic clusters, caches, distributed storage, sharding |

### Quick numeric before/after (4 -> 5 nodes)

| Scenario | Keys moved |
|----------|------------|
| Modulo rehash (key % N) | ~100% of keys reassigned |
| Consistent hashing (ideal) | ~1/5 ≈ 20% of keys reassigned |

---

## Practical details & examples

- Virtual nodes: To avoid uneven load (hot nodes), represent each real node by many virtual nodes (e.g., 100-200 points) distributed around the ring.
- Replication: For availability, store each key on its successor and the next R-1 successors (replication factor R).
- Node heterogeneity: Give nodes different numbers of virtual nodes proportional to capacity.
- Hash function: Use a stable, uniform hash (e.g., md5/sha1, or murmurhash). Keep the hash space size large enough to avoid clustering.

### Common pitfalls

- Not using virtual nodes -> imbalance and hotspots.
- Bad hash function or small hash space -> collisions and poor distribution.
- Forgetting replication -> losing availability when a node dies.
- Implementation that scans the whole ring linearly for lookups -> slow. Use a sorted structure + binary search.
- Expecting perfect balancing — consistent hashing gives probabilistic balance; tune virtual node count.

---

## Code example (Python) — minimal consistent hashing with virtual nodes

```python
import hashlib
import bisect

class ConsistentHashRing:
    def __init__(self, replicas=100):
        self.replicas = replicas
        self.ring = []        # sorted list of points
        self.nodes = {}       # point -> node

    def _hash(self, key):
        # return 32-bit int
        h = hashlib.md5(key.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
        return int(h, 16) & 0xffffffff

    def add_node(self, node_id):
        for i in range(self.replicas):
            point = self._hash(f'{node_id}:{i}')
            bisect.insort(self.ring, point)
            self.nodes[point] = node_id

    def remove_node(self, node_id):
        to_remove = []
        for i in range(self.replicas):
            point = self._hash(f'{node_id}:{i}')
            to_remove.append(point)
        for p in to_remove:
            idx = bisect.bisect_left(self.ring, p)
            if idx < len(self.ring) and self.ring[idx] == p:
                self.ring.pop(idx)
                del self.nodes[p]

    def get_node(self, key):
        if not self.ring:
            return None
        point = self._hash(key)
        idx = bisect.bisect(self.ring, point)
        if idx == len(self.ring):
            idx = 0
        return self.nodes[self.ring[idx]]

# Usage
ring = ConsistentHashRing(replicas=200)
ring.add_node('cache-A')
ring.add_node('cache-B')
ring.add_node('cache-C')
print(ring.get_node('user:1234'))

# When you add 'cache-D', only ~1/4 of keys move
ring.add_node('cache-D')
```

---

## When to use consistent hashing

- Distributed caches (Memcached / Redis clusters) to minimize cache misses after scale changes.
- Partitioning/sharding data across storage nodes when nodes are added/removed frequently.
- Load distribution in P2P systems or DHTs (e.g., BitTorrent, Cassandra)

## When not to use it

- Small static clusters where modulo hashing is sufficient and simpler.
- Systems where full rebalancing is acceptable and easy to manage.

---

## Mental model & checklist before implementing

- Do I need minimal key movement on topology changes? -> Use consistent hashing.
- Will node capacities differ? -> Use weighted virtual nodes.
- Need replication? -> Chain successors for R replicas.
- Will I have many small keys? -> Ensure uniform hash and enough virtual nodes.
keyTakeaways: Consistent hashing minimizes key movement on node add/remove (only ~1/N of keys move).
Use virtual nodes and a good hash to avoid load imbalance and hotspots.
Combine with replication and capacity weighting for availability and heterogeneity.
